body:
The "official" way to produce a no-threads build is to set `threads=no` when compiling.

`Max threads = 0` doesn't actually produce a no-threads build. It will still start threads occasionally in the thread pool, even if your fix https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123414 is merged. It is questionable what `Max threads = 0` is even for.

What's the reason you want to use `Max threads = 0` in the first place?

I am doing work on this PR:

[Add worker threads to BVH - #122686](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/122686)

One of the questions I have fielded is: "Will there be a way to disable this?". 

`Max Threads = 0` is the obvious way to disable it (rather than adding a setting). So that was my motivation to start looking.

However, now that I have looked into it, I think there are quite a few reasons that a soft-off could be helpful (given it is already there but just crashing):

* There is compilation time for `threads=no` which touches so many files (I won't use it much for that reason alone, I would rather just try to comment out some *.cpp code to achieve a test). 
* I like to test engine bugs using the exact same binary that is causing the bugs (the #ifdef's in `threads=no` remove a lot of code and kernel interactions). 
* Often I will want to step through the physics solver but I can't do it properly unless I can fully serialise the worker threads (this has been annoying in the past). 
* Profiling is another reason to turn off threads (while maybe leaving the pump task threads alone). 

From a user perspective:
* The average user won't necessarily want to be recompiling the engine and templates to deploy their game with `threads=no` if they need that.  
* If I didn't need the high performance (as a user), then I would turn off threading to save device power and improve background tasks. 
* Threading can be a source of engine bugs that may only show up in one game that stresses an untested pathway. I think it would be pretty common to want to try turning threads off (whether it helped or not). 

There may be other reasons, I am just speculating here.
